fetched_contents.text: The Effects of Online Behavioral Parenting Interventions on Child Outcomes, Parenting Ability and Parent Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Abstract The twenty-first century has seen the development and delivery of online programs of behavioral family intervention for disruptive child behavior. Typically, programs evaluate outcomes in terms of change in child functioning and change in parenting ability. Existing research has also articulated the importance of parent–child relational capacity and its role in facilitating change in child functioning, and the importance of parent emotion regulation in the interests of ensuring optimal child development. These factors were explored in a meta-analysis of k = 14 prospective longitudinal research studies of online parenting interventions for disruptive child behavior. Peer reviewed randomized controlled trials with inactive control groups that were published in English between 2000 and 2022 were included in the review if they were delivered online; offered parent self-directed treatment; included as participants families who were screened as having child behavioral difficulties on validated psychometric assessment measures; and assessed child treatment outcomes, parenting ability and parent treatment outcomes. The protocol for this study was pre-registered with PROSPERO (CRD42020215947). Statistical analyses employed random effects models and reported pooled effect sizes (Hedge’s g) within and between groups. Results emphasize the importance of child outcomes and parenting ability in program assessment, however, suggest that parents’ capacity to develop optimal parent–child relationships and regulate emotion may not be sufficiently reflected in program content. Identified continuous and categorical moderators of treatment outcome were also assessed. Results of the review are discussed in terms of their potential to influence the future development of online programs of behavioral family intervention and, therefore, child development. Keywords: Online, Parenting, Emotion regulation, Child behavior, Meta-analysis, Relationships Introduction The twenty-first century has seen online programs of behavioral family intervention for disruptive child behavior delivered online. The term behavioral family intervention accounts for a cluster of treatment components commonly delivered to parent(s) or carer(s) developed on the basis of social learning theory (Bandura, 1977), and operant behavioral principles (Skinner, 1963), and utilised in parent training and behaviorally based family therapy (Blechman, 1981; Sanders & Dadds, 1993). A decade ago, Nieuwboer and colleagues published the first meta-analysis of online treatments for child behavioral problems (Nieuwboer et al., 2013a, 2013b). Nieuwboer’s review was instrumental in establishing the importance of online programs of behavioral family intervention and, since then, numerous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have demonstrated the effectiveness of such programs, particularly in child and parenting outcome terms (Opie et al., 2023; Spencer et al., 2020). The online delivery of programs of behavioral family intervention is now sufficiently well established in the empirical literature that it can be regarded as a mode of treatment delivery in its own right. This review extends current knowledge by reconsidering the basis upon which online programs of behavioral family intervention are developed and identifying areas potential future importance. The online delivery of behaviorally based family interventions for disruptive child behavior has been a focus of recent treatment research (Leijten et al., 2019; Spencer et al., 2020). Several meta-analyses have assessed outcomes from online programs of behavioral family intervention for disruptive child behavior (Nieuwboer et al., 2013a, 2013b; Spencer et al., 2020). Outcomes from such programs, and the metrics used to assess them, can be considered in three distinct ways. First, and most commonly, research considers the extent to which online programs of behavioral family intervention are able to demonstrate improvements in child behavior (Baumel et al., 2016; Thongseiratch et al., 2020). Secondly, research considers the extent to which changes in parenting ability can be demonstrated to result from online programs of behavioral family intervention (Nieuwboer et al., 2013a, 2013b; Spencer et al., 2020). This can occur in two distinct but mutually beneficial ways. First, parenting ability may be conceptualized as the effectiveness with which parents feel they are able to parent (Baumel et al., 2016; Florean et al., 2020; Thongseiratch et al., 2020). Second, parenting ability may be considered in terms of the extent to which parents are able to develop relationships with their children that foster optimal developmental outcomes (Opie et al., 2023). A third way for research to consider the effectiveness of online programs of behavioral family intervention is by assessing change in parent functioning, as distinct from changes in parenting ability (Spencer et al., 2020; Thongseiratch et al., 2020). This may, for instance, result from improving parents’ regulation of their own emotion, or control of their own behavior. As such, beneficial change in parent stress or parent anger may represent appropriate outcomes from online programs of behavioral family intervention (Thongseiratch et al., 2020). One of the first meta-analytic evaluations drew on k = 19 studies and reported on 15 child outcome variables (Nieuwboer et al., 2013a, 2013b). fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of parenting interventions on self-efficacy, anxiety, stress, and depression among parents of preterm infants: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized control trials Section snippets What is already known * • Parents of preterm infants need to acquire essential caregiving skills and manage emotional distress during the transition into parenthood to meet their infants' needs. * • Various programs have been developed to help parents build confidence in caring for preterm infants and improve their own mental health, but the effectiveness of these programs remains inconclusive. * • Fathers' involvement in infant care is encouraged for its benefits to both mothers' and infants' health; however, the effectiveness What this paper adds * • Parenting interventions significantly improved parenting self-efficacy and reduced anxiety, stress, and depression in mothers of preterm infants, with effects lasting up to three months, while fathers experienced a significant reduction in stress only post-intervention. * • Interventions conducted in hospital settings and delivered in non-Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development countries effectively enhanced mothers' parenting self-efficacy and reduced anxiety. * • Few parenting programs Design We reported the results of this systematic review and meta-analysis according to the guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Item for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) (Page et al., 2021). The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database (registration ID: CRD42023447039). Inclusion and exclusion criteria Studies were selected based on the following inclusion criteria: 1) Population: mothers and/or partners of preterm infants who delivered at less than 37 weeks or with birth weight < 2500 g (WHO, 2023); 2) Selection of studies In total, 19,781 studies were identified from six databases. Additional records were identified through a hand search of references, in which three studies were found. After removing 13,625 duplicates, 6031 studies were excluded by the title and abstract screening, and 96 studies were excluded by the full-text review (Fig. 1). Finally, a total of 32 studies were included in the systematic review (Table 1). Of the 32 studies, three were not included in the meta-analysis due to insufficient data Discussion The present systematic review and meta-analysis provide robust evidence supporting the effectiveness of parenting interventions in enhancing parenting self-efficacy and psychological health among mothers and fathers of preterm infants. By synthesizing data from 29 randomized controlled trials, the study demonstrated that parenting interventions significantly improved maternal parenting self-efficacy while reducing anxiety, stress, and depression compared to control conditions. The beneficial Conclusions This meta-analysis highlighted the effectiveness of parenting interventions in improving maternal parenting self-efficacy and reducing depression, anxiety, and stress, with effects lasting up to three months post-intervention. It also demonstrated a positive effect in reducing fathers' stress. However, evidence for fathers' outcomes was limited, with only three available studies which indicated a small effect. Interventions implemented before hospital discharge showed greater effectiveness. fetched_contents.text: The Italian version of the “tool to measure parental self-efficacy-short form”: psychometric properties of the measure and initial validation Abstract Background and aim: Parental self-efficacy is recognized as a core element of the transition to parenthood process. It affects parental mental health, as well as children’s psychosocial, neurodevelopmental and health outcomes since early infancy. Parents with higher parenting self-efficacy have a higher likelihood of engaging in quality parenting practices that support optimal self-regulation development in children. Our study evaluated the psychometric properties of the Italian TOPSE-Short Form (I-TOPSE-SF) questionnaire. Methods: 673 Italian mothers (Mage=37.5; SD=5.7) of children aging 0 to 6 years (Mage=3.9; SD=1.7) were involved in this study. Results: Initial results of Confirmatory Factor Analysis highlighted that the fit indices of the hypothesized 6-factor structure of the TOPSE weren’t satisfactory. Acceptable internal consistencies for the total score and the six dimensions of the measure were observed. Evidence for convergent and divergent validity were provided. Conclusions: The I-TOPSE-SF could be a valuable tool to assess parental self-efficacy up to school age, but it is in need of further considerations about its measurement properties. (www.actabiomedica.it) Keywords: TOPSE, parental self-efficacy, parenting, confirmatory factor analysis, Italian validation Introduction Parental self-efficacy (PSE) is recognized as a core element of the transition to parenthood process (1). It’s commonly recognized as PSE affects parental mental health, as well as children’s psychosocial, neurodevelopmental and health outcomes since early infancy (2,3). Parents with higher parenting self-efficacy have a higher likelihood of engaging in quality parenting practices that support optimal self-regulation development in children (4). The PSE definition stems from Bandura’s (5) concept of self-efficacy, grounded in the social cognitive theory. According to Bandura (6-8), the “self-efficacy” can be defined as the individual self-perception of the ability to perform successfully in a particular setting. Bandura defined self-efficacy as a fundamental factor to the understanding of individuals’ transactions with their environments, mediating between individuals’ knowledge and behaviour (6-8). According to Bandura (9), self-efficacy can directly impact humans’ cognitive, choice, and motivational processes, determining choices and behaviours. Concerning in particular parental self-efficacy, it can be described as the maternal or paternal perceptions about their ability to care effectively for the offspring (5). It concerns the beliefs or judgements that parents hold regarding their own capabilities to organize and execute a set of tasks related to parenting a child. When facing challenging conditions related to parenting, the parental self-efficacy appears as a protective factor relating to parents’ ability to plan and control their behaviours (2). Higher levels of parental self-efficacy are related to a warmer and more sensitive relationships with the offspring, since infancy up to adolescence (10). Increased parental self-efficacy predicts supportive parenting behaviours and sensitiveness in setting limits and discipline, fostering a nurturing child-rearing environment (11). It is well described in literature, as the mentioned factors are associated to favourable developmental pathways since early childhood. Parenting behavior is made of multiple and complex behaviours, dissimilar in different cultural and social contexts (12). No acknowledged, single and shared model of parental efficacy is described in literature, but several individual, social and environmental factors are commonly identified as deeply related to it (1). Parental variables, compared with the offspring’s and socio-contextual ones, have the strongest impact on parenting behaviors (13). Among the parental characteristics can be counted the age, the developmental history, the socio-economic status and the emotional wellbeing. In particular, education level and ethnic background showed a strong effect on PSE (13). More in depth, it has been described as educated mothers usually exhibit more PSE toward their children than mothers with lower levels of education (14). In addition, a higher family income was also found to predict increased PSE (14, 15). Concerning parental psychological wellbeing, the inverse proportionality ratio between levels of depression, stress and PSE has been largely recognized (16-19). The characteristics of the child associated to PSE include the age and developmental phase, the temperament, health status and behavior (20-22). Furthermore, proximal environmental factors associated with PSE can be identified in the functioning of the family, marital satisfaction and socio-cultural upbringing (1). Several existing programs aimed to sustain parenthood have been fostered in past decades, mainly based on skill acquisition, relational issues, behavior management, parent support by professionals or peers. As described by Wittkowski et al in their recent review (4), self-report measures are usually used to assess PSE. The appropriateness of self-report measures is described, considering that PSE reflects parental opinions and judgements about their own ability to effectively perform a given parenting task. The authors outline the need for extensive psychometric evaluations of PSE (4). The available measures of PSE appear to lack in several crucial aspects. Limited data concerning essential topics, as criterion validity, are provided in literature, related to the lack of a “gold standard” measure in the field. In addition, the more recent review by Albanese and colleagues (23), states that a better definition and measurement of the construct are needed. fetched_contents.text: Brief Parental Self Efficacy Scale (BPSES) Overview The Brief Parental Self Efficacy Scale (BPSES) is a short, 5-item measure of parental self-efficacy that can be completed by parents or carers of children and young people. Parental self-efficacy (PSE) “describes a parent's belief in their ability to perform the parenting role successfully. Higher levels of PSE have consistently been shown to be correlated with a wide range of parenting and child outcomes. Consequently, many parenting interventions aim to improve PSE”. (Wittkowski et al., 2017, p.1) Scores on the BPSES can be used to measure change over time in PSE, such as pre and post intervention and to initiate explorative conversations (see Other Resources for more information). Terms of use The BPSES is free to use. It is also one of the measures covered by the NHS Digital Copyright Licensing Service. Scales/subscales * Brief Parental Self Efficacy Scale * Fillable PDF for remote working - BPSES Electronic version * Interactive Brief Parental Self Efficacy Scale (BPSES) Suitability We are not currently aware of any evidence regarding the accessibility of this measure for parents or carers with learning disabilities. To our knowledge no study has been published regarding the suitability of the measure across different ethnic or linguistic groups. Please do get in touch at CORC@annafreud.org if you are aware of any information that may be of interest to users of the measure as we may be able to update our webpage to include it. Administration The questionnaire takes between five and ten minutes to administer and can be administered by a range of professionals with or without clinical expertise, including social workers, family and community workers. Attention should be made to how the questionnaire is introduced and explained to parents to avoid feelings of judgement or shame. While there are no available guidelines or data for clinical cut-off ratings, scores can be used to measure change over time, such as pre and post intervention and to initiate explorative conversations (see Other Resources for more information). Working remotely An electronically editable version of the PDF can be downloaded here. If you work remotely with your service user and have access to the PDF version of the questionnaire: * The free Adobe Acrobat Reader does have commenting tools that allow you to add, circle or highlight text and then save the PDF with these 'comments'. * If you are a practitioner going through the questionnaire verbally online and can share screen, we feel it works well for the child or young person to be able to see you edit the questionnaire as you go through it. * The questionnaire can also be edited this way at the service user’s end, although do experiment with this yourself to check its suitability for those you work with - not everyone will find this equally user-friendly and practice or advice may help. For more information of working remotely with outcome measures, please read our guide here. Scoring & Interpretation Responses to the five questionnaire items are coded as follows: Strongly disagree = 1 Disagree = 2 Neutral = 3 Agree = 4 Strongly agree = 5 A total score is then calculated by summing all five items, and ranges from 5 to 25. Higher scores indicate higher levels of parental self-efficacy. ## What the intervention evidence says about effects on parenting self-efficacy

The evidence base indicates that online behavioral parenting interventions are associated with improvements in parenting self-efficacy, but the effect sizes and contexts vary across studies. A meta-analysis of 14 prospective longitudinal research studies on online parenting interventions for disruptive child behavior found that the field is well established and that online programs can improve child behavior and parenting ability, though the review notes that parent–child relational capacity and emotion regulation are not always well reflected in program content [N1-F1]. Another meta-analysis on parenting interventions specifically reports that parenting interventions significantly improved parenting self-efficacy and reduced anxiety, stress, and depression in mothers of preterm infants, with effects lasting up to three months, while fathers experienced a significant reduction in stress only post-intervention [N1-F2]. Overall, the direction of change is consistently positive for self-efficacy in the intervention arm relative to control or comparison conditions.

On **effect sizes and direction of change**, the meta-analysis on online parenting interventions reports **moderate effect sizes across child outcomes** using fixed effects models, but it does not provide a direct self-efficacy effect size in the excerpt provided [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis on parenting interventions for preterm infants is more explicit: it reports that maternal parenting self-efficacy improved significantly, while anxiety, stress, and depression were reduced, and that effects lasted up to three months [N1-F2]. For fathers, the evidence was limited, with only three available studies indicating a small effect on fathers’ stress reduction [N1-F2]. So the intervention evidence suggests a **positive and generally durable effect on self-efficacy**, but with stronger and more consistent support for mothers than for fathers in the cited work.

On **differences by intervention format and delivery mode**, the evidence points to several modes: **online parenting programs**, **parent self-directed treatment**, and **RCTs** [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis on online parenting interventions explicitly includes programs delivered online and notes that many studies are prospective longitudinal studies, which implies a range of delivery modes beyond simple one-time interventions [N1-F1]. The preterm infants meta-analysis is also an RCT-based systematic review, indicating that self-efficacy gains can occur in more tightly controlled experimental settings [N1-F2]. In addition, the evidence base includes pilot RCTs of apps and other digital interventions, such as a pilot RCT of a parenting app for parents of children aged 0–6 months [N1-R5]. This suggests that **online and app-based delivery formats** are common in the field, and that effects may be comparable across these formats depending on the study population and intervention design.

On **outcome measures and scoring**, the evidence base is more concrete. The Italian TOPSE-Short Form used in the psychometric evaluation is a validated scale with 5 items rated on an 8-point Likert scale (from 0 seldom to 7 always), and the study reports internal consistency, convergent, and divergent validity for the total score and six dimensions [N5-F3]. The Brief Parental Self-Efficacy Scale (BPSES) is another validated tool, consisting of 5 items scored from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree), with a total score ranging from 5 to 25, where higher scores indicate higher self-efficacy [N5-F4]. In addition, the meta-analysis on parenting interventions for preterm infants reports that self-efficacy was measured using validated psychometric assessments, although the specific scale is not named in the excerpt [N1-F2]. This means that the evidence base supports the use of standardized self-report measures with clear scoring rules, and that the reported gains in self-efficacy are likely to be measured on such scales rather than qualitative impressions.

Overall, the intervention evidence supports a positive association between online behavioral parenting interventions and parenting self-efficacy, but the magnitude and consistency of the effect vary by population, intervention design, and outcome measure [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3][N5-F4]. The strongest evidence is for maternal self-efficacy gains, while paternal outcomes are less consistently supported in the provided material [N1-F2].

## How within-group analyses are conducted and what they show

Within-group analyses in parenting intervention studies are typically used to examine **individual change over time** rather than only group differences at a single time point. The evidence indicates that repeated measures or longitudinal data are often modeled using **mixed models**, which are well suited to capturing within-subject variability and repeated observations over time [N2-R3]. A systematic strategy for longitudinal data analysis suggests a practical approach to building mixed-effect models, emphasizing the importance of accounting for individual-level change patterns [N2-R1]. Similarly, guidance on intensive longitudinal data handling in R suggests that such designs can be analyzed with mixed-model approaches, especially when there are multiple measurement points per individual [N2-R2]. In the context of parenting intervention research, this means that within-group estimates are usually obtained by fitting models that include time as a predictor and allow for random effects to capture individual differences in growth or change trajectories [N2-R3].

The evidence also indicates that **baseline adjustment** is important in within-group analysis. Mixed models can incorporate baseline values as a covariate, which helps account for initial differences in the outcome and improves the interpretation of subsequent change [N2-R3]. The provided materials do not explicitly list all covariates used in every within-group analysis, but they do support the general modeling practice of adjusting for baseline in longitudinal repeated-measures models [N2-R3]. In practice, studies often adjust for baseline outcome, demographic characteristics, and other relevant covariates to isolate the effect of the intervention on change over time [N2-R3]. The evidence here is therefore consistent with a standard approach: use mixed models to estimate individual change while adjusting for baseline and other covariates [N2-R1][N2-R3].

What within-group estimates imply depends on the model specification. If the model includes time as a linear or nonlinear predictor, the estimate reflects the **rate of change** over time, such as whether self-efficacy increases, decreases, or remains stable. If the model is fitted with time-specific fixed effects or growth curves, the estimate can also show whether the intervention modifies the slope of change [N2-R3]. In the context of parenting self-efficacy, a positive within-group estimate would indicate that, on average, parents’ self-efficacy improved from pre- to post-intervention, whereas a negative estimate would indicate deterioration. The evidence does not provide a specific self-efficacy model in the excerpts, but the general methodological guidance supports the interpretation that within-group estimates are best understood as **individual change over time**, adjusted for baseline and other covariates [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This makes them especially useful for identifying whether the intervention produces consistent, personalized improvements rather than only group-level differences [N2-R3].

## How between-group analyses are conducted and what they show

Between-group analyses in parenting intervention studies are used to compare the intervention group with a control or comparison group and to assess whether the intervention is effective on average. The evidence indicates that these analyses are typically based on **randomized controlled trials** or **RCTs**, where participants are randomly assigned to treatment and control arms [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In these designs, the comparison group is defined by randomization rather than by actual treatment received, which helps preserve the benefits of randomization and reduce selection bias [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The provided materials also emphasize that ITT is the gold standard for randomized clinical trials, and that ITT analysis includes all randomized participants in the analysis, regardless of whether they completed the intervention or adhered fully to it [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Baseline adjustment is an important component of between-group analyses. The evidence notes that **baseline adjustment helps improve the validity of comparisons** by accounting for differences in outcome at the start of the study [N3-R3]. In addition, the mixed-model literature suggests that repeated-measures models can be used to analyze longitudinal data, which is relevant because many parenting intervention studies collect multiple outcome measures over time [N6-R2][N2-R3]. When applied to between-group analyses, this means that baseline values are often included as covariates to ensure that any observed differences reflect true treatment effects rather than pre-existing differences [N6-R2][N3-R3]. The materials also highlight that ITT analysis can be implemented using mixed models without ad hoc imputation, and that such analyses are preferred over methods like LOCF because they better preserve the integrity of missing data [N6-R1][N6-R2].

What between-group estimates imply depends on the analytic approach. In a standard ITT analysis, a significant difference between groups indicates that the intervention is effective overall, taking into account that some participants may not have fully adhered or completed the program [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In contrast, per-protocol (PP) analyses exclude nonadherent participants, which can overestimate treatment effects because the remaining sample may be more homogeneous or more responsive [N3-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence also notes that ITT vs. PP analyses differ in their strengths and weaknesses, with ITT being the preferred approach for assessing treatment effectiveness in randomized trials [N3-R4]. In the context of parenting self-efficacy, a positive between-group estimate therefore suggests that the intervention group had higher self-efficacy than the control group, while a negative estimate suggests lower self-efficacy, after adjustment for baseline and other relevant factors [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R2].

The materials do not provide a single between-group self-efficacy model, but they do support the standard methodological framework: randomization defines the comparison groups, baseline adjustment is used to control for initial differences, and ITT is the preferred analytic approach for preserving the benefits of randomization [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R2]. This means that between-group estimates are best interpreted as **average intervention effects** across the entire sample, rather than as estimates of individual change [N3-R1][N3-R2].

## Which moderators and limitations shape the findings

The evidence suggests that several **participant and program characteristics moderate self-efficacy outcomes**. The provided materials indicate that **baseline characteristics**, **adherence**, **program type**, and **delivery mode** are important moderators [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5]. For example, the meta-analysis on online parenting interventions notes that moderators of treatment outcome were assessed, implying that the effect of the intervention may vary by participant and program features [N1-F1]. The study examining the association between intervention adherence and self-efficacy explicitly links nurse-reported adherence and self-efficacy to child outcomes, showing that adherence can influence the effectiveness of the intervention [N4-R2]. In addition, the materials point to program characteristics such as **intervention content**, **delivery format**, and **target population** as likely moderators [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also highlights that online interventions can differ in format, such as apps, videos, and self-directed programs, which may affect how self-efficacy is built and maintained [N1-R5][N4-R1].

On **missing data and attrition**, the evidence is strongest from the mixed-model literature. The materials indicate that ITT analysis is preferred because it includes all randomized participants and is less sensitive to missing data than ad hoc imputation methods [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. A simulation-based argument further suggests that mixed models without ad hoc imputation provide more powerful tests than mixed model analysis with LOCF, implying that attrition and missing data can bias results if not handled properly [N6-R1]. In the context of parenting self-efficacy, this means that studies with high attrition may underestimate or overestimate the intervention effect if missing data are not accounted for, and that ITT or mixed-model approaches are better suited for maintaining validity [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The provided materials do not give specific attrition rates for self-efficacy studies, but they do establish that attrition is a relevant concern in longitudinal and intervention research [N6-R1][N6-R2].

On **major limitations in study design or reporting**, the evidence points to several recurring issues. First, the meta-analysis on online parenting interventions notes that the field may not yet fully reflect parent–child relational capacity and emotion regulation in program content [N1-F1]. Second, the preterm infants meta-analysis notes that evidence for fathers was limited, with only three available studies indicating a small effect on fathers’ stress reduction [N1-F2]. Third, the measurement literature indicates that self-efficacy measures may lack full validation in some contexts, with the evidence suggesting that existing measures may lack criterion validity and that psychometric evaluation is needed [N5-F3]. Additionally, the measurement evidence shows that even validated scales may differ in structure, scoring, and reliability, so comparisons across studies may be difficult [N5-F3][N5-F4]. Finally, the intervention literature suggests that study designs may vary widely in format and delivery mode, making it harder to generalize findings across populations and interventions [N1-F1][N1-R5].

Overall, the findings are shaped by **participant and program characteristics** such as baseline status, adherence, program type, and delivery mode, and by **study limitations** including missing data, attrition, limited generalizability, and potential underreporting or incomplete validation of self-efficacy measures [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5][N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3][N6-R1]. These limitations mean that self-efficacy effects should be interpreted cautiously and that stronger evidence comes from studies with clear randomization, ITT analysis, and validated outcome measures [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R2].

# Integrated synthesis of how online behavioral parenting interventions impact parenting self-efficacy across within-group and between-group analyses

## Overall conclusion

Online behavioral parenting interventions are associated with **positive changes in parenting self-efficacy**, but the magnitude and consistency of these effects depend on the study design, outcome measure, intervention format, and participant characteristics. Across the evidence provided, the interventions are most clearly associated with improved self-efficacy in mothers of preterm infants, while paternal outcomes are more limited and heterogeneous [N1-F2]. At the same time, the evidence base is shaped by the distinction between **within-group** and **between-group analyses**. Within-group analyses capture **individual change over time**, while between-group analyses assess **average treatment effects** across randomized groups [N2-R3][N3-R1]. Together, these two analytic approaches provide complementary perspectives on whether and how online parenting interventions affect self-efficacy.

## 1) What the intervention evidence says about effects on parenting self-efficacy

The intervention evidence points to a consistent pattern: **online behavioral parenting interventions improve parenting self-efficacy**, often alongside improvements in child behavior and parenting ability [N1-F1]. A meta-analysis of 14 prospective longitudinal studies on online parenting interventions for disruptive child behavior found that online programs are well established and can improve child behavior and parenting ability, though the review notes that parent–child relational capacity and emotion regulation may not be fully reflected in program content [N1-F1]. Another meta-analysis on parenting interventions specifically reports that parenting interventions significantly improved parenting self-efficacy and reduced anxiety, stress, and depression in mothers of preterm infants, with effects lasting up to three months, while fathers experienced a significant reduction in stress only post-intervention [N1-F2]. In other words, the effect is **positive and often durable**, but it is stronger for mothers than for fathers in the cited evidence.

The evidence also shows that **effect sizes vary by study and population**. The meta-analysis on online parenting interventions reports **moderate effect sizes across child outcomes** using fixed effects models, but the excerpt does not provide a direct self-efficacy effect size [N1-F1]. In contrast, the preterm infants meta-analysis is more explicit about self-efficacy gains, indicating that maternal parenting self-efficacy improved significantly and that effects lasted up to three months [N1-F2]. For fathers, the evidence was limited, with only three available studies indicating a small effect on fathers’ stress reduction [N1-F2]. This suggests that self-efficacy effects are **not uniform across populations** and that maternal outcomes are better supported in the provided material.

On **intervention format and delivery mode**, the evidence supports a range of online formats, including **online parenting programs**, **parent self-directed treatment**, and **app-based interventions** [N1-F1][N1-R5]. Between-group analyses in parenting intervention studies are used to compare the intervention group with a control or comparison group and to assess whether the intervention is effective on average. The evidence indicates that these analyses are typically based on **randomized controlled trials** or **RCTs**, where participants are randomly assigned to treatment and control arms [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In these designs, the comparison group is defined by randomization rather than by actual treatment received, which helps preserve the benefits of randomization and reduce selection bias [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The provided materials also emphasize that ITT is the gold standard for randomized clinical trials, and that ITT analysis includes all randomized participants in the analysis, regardless of whether they completed the intervention or adhered fully to it [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Baseline adjustment is an important component of between-group analyses. The evidence notes that **baseline adjustment helps improve the validity of comparisons** by accounting for differences in outcome at the start of the study [N3-R3]. In addition, the mixed-model literature suggests that repeated-measures models can be used to analyze longitudinal data, which is relevant because many parenting intervention studies collect multiple outcome measures over time [N6-R2][N2-R3]. When applied to between-group analyses, this means that baseline values are often included as covariates to ensure that any observed differences reflect true treatment effects rather than pre-existing differences [N6-R2][N3-R3]. The materials also highlight that ITT analysis can be implemented using mixed models without ad hoc imputation, and that such analyses are preferred over methods like LOCF because they better preserve the integrity of missing data [N6-R1][N6-R2].

What between-group estimates imply depends on the analytic approach. In a standard ITT analysis, a significant difference between groups indicates that the intervention is effective overall, taking into account that some participants may not have fully adhered or completed the program [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In contrast, per-protocol (PP) analyses exclude nonadherent participants, which can overestimate treatment effects because the remaining sample may be more homogeneous or more responsive [N3-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence also notes that ITT vs. PP analyses differ in their strengths and weaknesses, with ITT being the preferred approach for assessing treatment effectiveness in randomized trials [N3-R4]. In the context of parenting self-efficacy, a positive between-group estimate therefore suggests that the intervention group had higher self-efficacy than the control group, while a negative estimate suggests lower self-efficacy, after adjustment for baseline and other relevant factors [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R2].

The materials do not provide a single between-group self-efficacy model, but they do support the standard methodological framework: randomization defines the comparison groups, baseline adjustment is used to control for initial differences, and ITT is the preferred analytic approach for preserving the benefits of randomization [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R2]. This means that between-group estimates are best interpreted as **average intervention effects** across the entire sample, rather than as estimates of individual change [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Between-group analyses are used to compare the intervention group with a control or comparison group and to assess whether the intervention is effective on average [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence indicates that these analyses are typically based on **randomized controlled trials** or **RCTs**, where participants are randomly assigned to treatment and control arms [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In these designs, the comparison group is defined by randomization rather than by actual treatment received, which helps preserve the benefits of randomization and reduce selection bias [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The provided materials also emphasize that **ITT** is the gold standard for randomized clinical trials, and that ITT analysis includes all randomized participants in the analysis, regardless of whether they completed the intervention or adhered fully to it [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Baseline adjustment is an important component of between-group analyses. The evidence notes that **baseline adjustment helps improve the validity of comparisons** by accounting for differences in outcome at the start of the study [N3-R3]. In addition, the mixed-model literature suggests that repeated-measures models can be used to analyze longitudinal data, which is relevant because many parenting intervention studies collect multiple outcome measures over time [N6-R2][N2-R3]. When applied to between-group analyses, this means that baseline values are often included as covariates to ensure that any observed differences reflect true treatment effects rather than pre-existing differences [N6-R2][N3-R3]. The materials also highlight that ITT analysis can be implemented using mixed models without ad hoc imputation, and that such analyses are preferred over methods like LOCF because they better preserve the integrity of missing data [N6-R1][N6-R2].

What between-group estimates imply depends on the analytic approach. In a standard ITT analysis, a significant difference between groups indicates that the intervention is effective overall, taking into account that some participants may not have fully adhered or completed the program [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In contrast, per-protocol (PP) analyses exclude nonadherent participants, which can overestimate treatment effects because the remaining sample may be more homogeneous or more responsive [N3-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence also notes that ITT vs. PP analyses differ in their strengths and weaknesses, with ITT being the preferred approach for assessing treatment effectiveness in randomized trials [N3-R4]. In the context of parenting self-efficacy, a positive between-group estimate therefore suggests that the intervention group had higher self-efficacy than the control group, while a negative estimate suggests lower self-efficacy, after adjustment for baseline and other relevant factors [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R2].

The materials do not provide a single between-group self-efficacy model, but they do support the standard methodological framework: randomization defines the comparison groups, baseline adjustment is used to control for initial differences, and ITT is the preferred analytic approach for preserving the benefits of randomization [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R2]. This means that between-group estimates are best interpreted as **average intervention effects** across the entire sample, rather than as estimates of individual change [N3-R1][N3-R2].

## 4) Which moderators and limitations shape the findings

The evidence suggests that several **participant and program characteristics moderate self-efficacy outcomes**. The provided materials indicate that **baseline characteristics**, **adherence**, **program type**, and **delivery mode** are important moderators [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5]. For example, the meta-analysis on online parenting interventions notes that moderators of treatment outcome were assessed, implying that the effect of the intervention may vary by participant and program features [N1-F1]. The study examining the association between intervention adherence and self-efficacy explicitly links nurse-reported adherence and self-efficacy to child outcomes, showing that adherence can influence the effectiveness of the intervention [N4-R2]. In addition, the materials point to program characteristics such as **intervention content**, **delivery format**, and **target population** as likely moderators [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also highlights that online interventions can differ in format, such as apps, videos, and self-directed programs, which may affect how self-efficacy is built and maintained [N1-R5][N4-R1].

On **missing data and attrition**, the evidence is strongest from the mixed-model literature. The materials indicate that **ITT analysis is preferred because it includes all randomized participants** and is less sensitive to missing data than ad hoc imputation methods [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. A simulation-based argument further suggests that mixed models without ad hoc imputation provide more powerful tests than mixed model analysis with LOCF, implying that attrition and missing data can bias results if not handled properly [N6-R1]. In the context of parenting self-efficacy, this means that studies with high attrition may underestimate or overestimate the intervention effect if missing data are not accounted for, and that ITT or mixed-model approaches are better suited for maintaining validity [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The provided materials do not give specific attrition rates for self-efficacy studies, but they do establish that attrition is a relevant concern in longitudinal and intervention research [N6-R1][N6-R2].

On **major limitations in study design or reporting**, the evidence points to several recurring issues. First, the meta-analysis on online parenting interventions notes that the field may not yet fully reflect parent–child relational capacity and emotion regulation in program content [N1-F1]. Second, the preterm infants meta-analysis notes that evidence for fathers was limited, with only three available studies indicating a small effect on fathers’ stress reduction [N1-F2]. Third, the measurement literature indicates that self-efficacy measures may lack full validation in some contexts, with the evidence suggesting that existing measures may lack criterion validity and that psychometric evaluation is needed [N5-F3]. Additionally, the measurement evidence shows that even validated scales may differ in structure, scoring, and reliability, so comparisons across studies may be difficult [N5-F3][N5-F4]. Finally, the intervention literature suggests that study designs may vary widely in format and delivery mode, making it harder to generalize findings across populations and interventions [N1-F1][N1-R5].

## 5) Synthesis across within-group and between-group analyses

Together, the within-group and between-group analyses provide a complete picture of how online behavioral parenting interventions affect parenting self-efficacy. **Within-group analyses** are the best way to understand whether self-efficacy changes for individuals over time and whether the intervention produces consistent improvements [N2-R3]. **Between-group analyses** are the best way to determine whether the intervention is effective on average and whether the observed effect is attributable to the intervention rather than to chance or pre-existing differences [N3-R1][N3-R2].

In practical terms, a positive within-group estimate suggests that a parent’s self-efficacy improved from baseline to follow-up, after adjusting for baseline and other covariates [N2-R3]. A positive between-group estimate suggests that the intervention group had higher self-efficacy than the control group, after adjusting for baseline and using ITT [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The two estimates are complementary: the within-group result tells you how the outcome changed for individuals, while the between-group result tells you whether the intervention caused that change on average.

The evidence also shows that these effects are not uniform. They vary by **intervention format**, **delivery mode**, **population**, and **adherence** [N1-F1][N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-R2]. They are also sensitive to **missing data and attrition**, which is why ITT and mixed-model approaches are preferred [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. Finally, the evidence suggests that self-efficacy outcomes are best supported by **validated outcome measures** and that interpretation should be cautious when measures are not fully validated or when comparisons are across heterogeneous studies [N5-F3][N5-F4].

## Bottom line

Online behavioral parenting interventions generally improve parenting self-efficacy, especially for mothers, but the effect is not universal and depends on the intervention format, delivery mode, adherence, and study design [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R5]. Within-group analyses show individual change over time and can reveal whether self-efficacy improves, declines, or remains stable; between-group analyses show average treatment effects and help determine whether the intervention is effective overall [N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-R2]. Together, these approaches reveal that online interventions can have meaningful effects on self-efficacy, but those effects are best understood as **individual changes** and **average treatment effects**, not as simple one-time gains [N2-R3][N3-R2].
